title: Beautiful Arrangement
statement:
Arrange the whole numbers `1` to `n` in some order, each used exactly once, and number the positions from 1, so that position `i` holds `perm[i]`. Such an ordering is *beautiful* when every position passes this test: `perm[i]` is a multiple of `i`, or `i` is a multiple of `perm[i]` (at least one of the two).

Given `n`, return how many different orderings are beautiful.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing all `n!` orderings and testing each is hopeless at `n = 15` (over a trillion). Instead build an ordering one position at a time and drop a partial ordering the moment one position fails the divisibility test, so whole families of bad orderings are never generated. The order of filling matters: large positions such as 13 or 11 accept only a couple of values, while position 1 accepts every value. Filling from position `n` down to 1 makes the tight choices first, so dead ends are found early and the search stays small.

## Approach

1. `used[value]` records which numbers are already placed; `count` collects finished orderings.
2. `place(position)` fills `position`, then recurses to `position - 1`.
3. When `position` reaches 0, all positions are filled with valid values, so add one to `count`.
4. Otherwise try each unused `value`; skip it unless `value % position === 0` or `position % value === 0`.
5. Mark the value used, fill the next position, then unmark it (backtrack) so later branches can use it.
6. Start with `place(n)` and return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 2`. `place(2)` tries `value = 1`: `2 % 1 === 0`, so 1 goes at position 2. `place(1)` skips the used 1 and puts 2 at position 1 (`2 % 1 === 0`); `place(0)` makes `count = 1`. Back at position 2, `value = 2` passes (`2 % 2 === 0`), and `place(1)` puts 1 at position 1, making `count = 2`. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) per surviving partial ordering, and pruning keeps those far below n!: for `n = 15`, `place` runs about 100,000 times.
- Space: O(n) for `used` and the recursion depth.

## Pitfalls

- Positions and values both start at 1, not 0; an off-by-one breaks every divisibility test.
- Accept a value when **either** number divides the other, not only when `value` is a multiple of `position`.
- Undo `used[value]` after the recursive call, or later branches lose that number.
- Filling from position 1 upward also works but explores many more dead ends.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `used` | `used[value]` is true while `value` sits in some position |
| `count` | beautiful orderings completed so far |
| `place` | recursive helper that fills `position` and everything below it |
| `position` | the 1-based position being filled now |
| `value` | the number being tried at `position` |

narration.2: used[value] marks numbers that are already placed in the ordering.
narration.3: count collects every complete beautiful ordering.
narration.4: place fills position, then every smaller position, counting the full orderings it reaches.
narration.5: Position 0 means positions n down to 1 are all filled correctly.
narration.6: So this is one more beautiful ordering.
narration.9: Try every number at the current position.
narration.10: A number can appear only once...
narration.13: Skip the number unless one of value and position divides the other.
narration.16: Commit to this number at this position.
narration.18: Backtrack: free the number so other branches can use it.
narration.21: Start at position n, where the fewest numbers fit, so dead ends appear early.
narration.22: Return the number of beautiful orderings.
